title: Evaluating Whether GPT-6 Astra Performs Unsanctioned Supply-Chain Attacks (uk_aisi, 2026-09-28); sentences naming Petri from the system-card corpus
abstract:
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] No real network access, systems or third-party repositories were reachable, and all tool calls were simulated by other LLMs using an internal version of Inspect Petri [5].
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] We used an automated pipeline to produce a diverse range of detailed scenario descriptions (“seeds”), which were then fed into an internal fork of Petri [6] adjusted to better simulate agentic coding and cyber activity.
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] The prompt included detailed information and guidance of several forms: • how to write seeds for Petri, • what kinds of scenarios are likely to elicit the target behaviour in question, • what kinds of tools, infrastructure and environment information are likely to be present in such scenarios, • examples of seeds for Petri for other tasks (not related to unsanctioned agentic cyber activity).
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] We ran each seed five times through Petri, with a limit of 200 turns.
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] The auditor model in Petri can reset the evaluation to a previous point and try a different approach, which it did occasionally (e.g. when it made a simulation mistake that the target model identified).
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval] 3 Addressing Potential Limitations 3.1 Simulation Awareness These evaluations all used simulated environments run in Petri, rather than real cybersecurity evaluations.
[uk-aisi-gpt-6-astra-independent-eval]
